speechtext:
On the orders of the day:
Hon. Gordon Churchill (Winnipeg South
Centre): I should like to direct a question to the Minister of National Defence. Does the minister consider that military information published by NORAD is classified and therefore not to be published in Canada?
Hon. Paul Hellyer (Minister of National
Defence): If the information is published it is unclassified.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: ALLEGED DENIAL BY MINISTER OF INFORMATION PUBLISHED ELSEWHERE
speechtext:
Then I have to rise on a question of privilege and draw the attention of the house to the fact that in an answer given yesterday the minister stated that classified information was required in an answer to two questions and therefore it could not be made public. I refer to page 2034 of Hansard, the second column, to a question asked by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam. The first part of the question reads as follows:
As of January 1 each year from 1957 to 1963, how many Soviet bombers, by types, have been estimated capable of making at least a one way attack on the main industrial areas of southern Canada and the northern United States?
The answer given by the minister is:
Since the information requested is classified it should be appreciated that it would not be in the public interest for the government to answer these questions.
I have in front of me a copy of a publication by headquarters, North American air defence command, office of information, called "The NORAD Story" published in the spring of 1961, in which occur these sentences:
The Soviets now have 1,200 first line jets in their bomber force. Mr. Khrushchev says that they do not 

intend to build any more. Even if they don't, the Soviets, by cannibalizing parts, could still have an attack force of more than 500 of these atomic carriers as late as 1970 . . . Those 500 bombers could dump an estimated 1,000 megatons of destructive energy on this continent.
In the Ottawa Journal of April 1, 1963 Mr. Dave McIntosh states:
North American air defence command estimates that Russia has 1,000 bombers that could reach North American targets.
Then he names the types. The minister tells us that this information is classified, yet we get the information from other sources. He says that if NORAD publishes it, it is not classified. Consequently the house is being misled with regard to essential information.

subtopic: ALLEGED DENIAL BY MINISTER OF INFORMATION PUBLISHED ELSEWHERE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on this question the figures which the hon. gentleman has just read are, of course, approximations, or if I may use the expression used the other day in the committee, ball park figures. They are not precise figures; therefore they are not, as he has said, classified. The question put on the order paper by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam asked for specific information in respect to quantities and types of aircraft, and if I had produced figures which were rounded and not accurate, and any person could have substantiated the fact that they were not accurate, then I would have been accused of misleading the house.
It is not the practice to produce exact information in respect to the Soviet threat. It is not produced on an unclassified basis by NORAD, nor is it produced in Canada on an unclassified basis, and I am sure my hon. friend is very much aware of this. There was no misleading whatsoever. We cannot produce exact figures; therefore it was impossible to answer the question in the form in which it was asked.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: ALLEGED DENIAL BY MINISTER OF INFORMATION PUBLISHED ELSEWHERE
speechtext: I have a supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. subtopic: ALLEGED DENIAL BY MINISTER OF INFORMATION PUBLISHED ELSEWHERE
speechtext: As I indicated before, they would be approximations, as was the case with the rounded number in respect to the number of Soviet submarines.

One reason for my intervention at this time is that the hon. gentleman has indicated that he is tempted to speak again on this bill. Perhaps if the Secretary of State would agree not to speak further on it I should not myself feel tempted to take part in the debate. However, far be it from any member representing the Atlantic provinces to discourage the hon. gentleman from speaking again on a measure which is of such great importance to our area. Indeed, I believe it is of paramount importance that the Secretary of State should speak again in this debate because there are some matters, especially those related to the personnel of the board, which are deserving of further clarification not only for the benefit of hon. members but also for the benefit of those people who have accepted these positions. These are gentlemen who through no fault of their own find that their appointments are cut short because there has been a general election and a political party has come to office which apparently has not looked too kindly on appointments made by the former government.
This appears to be the sum and substance of the reasons this government had in mind for deleting a number of years from the length of appointment of these board members. It seems to me that this action in cutting short the term of appointments constitutes an affront to these individuals, and that the Secretary of State owes them some better explanation than he has so far given.
I should like to know from the hon. gentleman whether he has received any correspondence from the individuals in question. If so,
I should like to know what representations they have made.

speechtext: Could I ask the hon. member a question? Is it the purpose of his speech to try to make it impossible for the present members of the board to continue? He is doing his best to create a situation of disharmony, and I hope he fails.

speechtext:
Let me say that with the length of time they have it would not make much difference if they were there or not. If the hon. member is going to tell this house that the problems of the Atlantic provinces can be solved in a year, which is all the time they will have as members of the board, then he is as crazy as a hoot owl. The difficulties of the Atlantic provinces are not beyond solution, but it will take a longer time than that to deal with them. We started on the road to salvation. I am concerned about what will happen under this administration.
I am concerned about the way in which they are tackling what is the most significant piece of legislation to make it possible for

us to lift ourselves up and bring ourselves to a level with the rest of the Canadian nation.
As I have said, I do not think the Secretary of State has been fair to these gentlemen. I think he should say to them, we thought we would appoint you for a year to try to get over the accusation that we are being political partisans and that you are political partisans, and he knows he cannot prove that latter statement. So he is trying to push them out gently. The Secretary of State says I am causing disharmony. What greater disharmony could there be than is being caused by this legislation and especially by clause 4. How much more difficult will it be for any government in the future to get men who have great contributions to make to our area to serve on government boards if they are to have fears that they will be involved in political hassles when governments change?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MEMBERSHIP, FUNDS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext: You are involving them.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MEMBERSHIP, FUNDS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
I am involving them, someone says. Let me tell him that his government involved them. I had nothing to do with it. I would have said nothing about these appointments. I would have said nothing about the new appointments if you people had not brought in this amendment. That is the reason I am talking now, because I hope that even at this late date the Secretary of State and the men around him will see the folly of their ways and correct them by allowing the men who he is convinced should serve to serve the full length of time which was promised to them. That is really an insignificant request of the government, and I am asking it on behalf of gentlemen who have given so much to our area already and are able and capable of giving so much more in the years ahead. These men will hesitate in future to get involved in government appointments to any board if this is the type of shoddy treatment given them because a government not of the same political stripe as this one happened to appoint them to their positions.
We have, Mr. Speaker, an awful lot of barkers on the other side of the house. They were over there until 1957 and they barked a lot. Then they came over here and barked some more, and now they are back there barking again like the trained seals they were before 1957 and are still, and they will probably never change. They will let a bunch of front benchers run the party, bring in outside consultants for anything and everything, and write budgets which have to be redressed, undressed and everything else. But they do not say very much or contribute much to the debates of this house.

There is another matter on which I want to hear from the Secretary of State. He is a pretty clever individual with words, and I only wish I were as clever. However, I did not spend as much time at university as he did, perhaps, and my vocabulary did not grow as large as his. I hope he will understand my plain language, though, when I ask him for a plain statement of fact in ordinary words about the Chignecto complex and what is to be done about it. I note that the President of the United States has indicated that the Passamaquoddy project and the tidal power associated with it is to be reopened for negotiations and further talks. We in Canada have more potential tidal power available at a cheaper rate, and I should like to know what we are going to do about it.
I have asked the Secretary of State about this two or three times. He always answers my questions, but in such a way that you never know whether it is going to remain latent, as it is at the present time, or whether he is going to put the Atlantic development board into high gear and get them moving on the Chignecto complex. Six years wasted, my hon. friend says. That is just how little he knows about it. I do not want any ifs, buts, or "I will tell so and so, or ask so and so, and see what he says". He is a member of the government and the spokesman for the Atlantic development board. I want to know from him, and I am sure the people of the Atlantic provinces would like to know, just exactly what they are going to do. Are they going to carry out an examination of the tides of the bay of Fundy, or are they not? It is not a difficult question and can be answered yes or no. He is certainly in a position to tell the Atlantic development board to carry out such an investigation. He can also tell them not to, and in a few weeks' time when he has made these new appointments he can probably tell them to stall as well, whenever he wants to. But I feel that the Atlantic provinces should know, and know in no uncertain terms, whether such an investigation is going to be carried out.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that when we hear from the Secretary of State about the appointment of these men he will tell us that they will be continued in office for the terms for which they were appointed originally. If he does not do so why does he bother

Actually the short space of time they will be sitting on the board under this legislation will not really allow them the chance to make the type of contribution they could make were they there for the period of time for which they were first appointed.
I also think it is unfair for the Secretary of State to say "Oh, these men can be reappointed". speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall be very brief in my remarks, as usual. I should like to say I repudiate and resent very much the suggestion of the Secretary of State that my hon. friend, colleague and neighbour, the hon. member for Cumberland, would either by his actions or by his remarks do anything which would bring disharmony to any move to advance the welfare of the maritime provinces. His record has been well established and I do not have to cite the facts relating thereto.
This has been a very interesting debate, Mr. Speaker. However, if I have any regret it is for the fact that yesterday the chairman cut off the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre when he was cataloguing the virtues of the many native maritimers who had won great acclaim for Canada. However, had he gone on to complete the full list perhaps we would never have completed what we did yesterday.
I have one small matter, small only in terms of the length of my remarks and not otherwise, and I mention it because it is of great importance. I have been seeking in this session by questions directed to the Minister of Public Works and the Prime Minister, and at other times, to get a clear statement


from the present government in respect to that great national project, the Prince Edward Island causeway. I have asked the Secretary of State to give us the clear assurance that this major project is one which will not be considered by the board because the decision relating to its construction taken by the former government will be upheld and carried out by the present government.
I have not yet obtained that information, and I might say that despite having sought information on the Prince Edward Island causeway several times from various members of the government I have elicited absolutely no information. The only information one can obtain is through press releases emanating from the Solicitor General (Mr. MacNaught) who, as far as I know, does not have administrative responsibility for this important function.
I think information sought in the House of Commons should be given in the House of Commons, and I recall that the former prime minister made a concise, precise and definite statement in respect of this project when he said that the causeway would be built. This is the kind of thing we hope to have from the present government. I am delighted to read the press releases from the Solicitor General. He is my neighbour. In fact had I been born a mile further west I would have had the pleasure of voting against him in Prince county. I read with interest everything he gives to the newspapers and I regard him highly, but I should still like to hear from the minister in charge or the Prime Minister exactly what is going to be done in respect of the causeway; and I trust that the Secretary of State, who used to be so deeply interested in this project, will tell us whether the causeway is going ahead.

The Atlantic provinces economic council has from time to time made assessments of the number of jobs that will be needed in the Atlantic provinces over the next 10 years not only to absorb new entrants into the labour force but also to reduce the level of unemployment in the Atlantic provinces to a comparable national level. That number of new jobs required is large. It can only be reached by the development of a coordinated plan over a period of years, directed to the various industries and directed to proposals that will provide these jobs in these

The minister spoke at great length about the famous Gordon commission report on the maritime provinces, and he spoke about what the hon. member for Queens had said in this regard. Well, as I stated in the budget debate, we all know what the Minister of Finance said in the famous Gordon report. It was even so famous in the maritime provinces that he had to come to my constituency, I think in 1961, and make another Gordon report at the Sutherlands River rural high school. At that time he said "I did not really mean to say they had to move out. I meant" this, that, and the other thing. But, as I said in the budget debate, we are leery of the Minister of Finance. He is the man controlling the purse strings, and I hope the Minister of Labour has a lot of influence with the Minister of Finance in order to help our area. I am sure we were glad to have the former minister of finance from Nova Scotia, who helped us a great deal. I hope the Minister of Labour is really in thick, as we say in the maritime provinces, with the present Minister of Finance.
The minister said that the only new thing brought forward in the twenty fourth parliament was the Atlantic adjustment grants. That was new. The minister is a little older than I, although not too much older, and he may not have been in the government through the years here in Ottawa. I remember that great leader of the province of Nova Scotia, Hon. Angus L. Macdonald, who was respected by everybody and who was a great friend of all Nova Scotians. He also did a great job here in wartime as minister of naval affairs. For many years he came to Ottawa seeking adjustment grants in order to bring the Atlantic provinces up to the level of the other provinces of Canada, and he was turned down. I do not know whether the minister was here during the last few years when his friend, who was premier for a short time, Mr. Henry Hicks, who is now president of a university, also came to Ottawa and returned with empty hands. The Atlantic adjustment grants were new, as the minister said. If they were the only new thing accomplished in that parliament it was certainly worth while electing a Conservative government under the Leader of the Opposition during that period.
The minister also spoke of the matter of the coastguard. He said, if I am quoting him correctly, that all we did was put a few coats of paint on existing ships. We brought forward a new coastguard plan. I would tell the minister-he has probably heard it before-that tenders were called for coastguard ships which were 95 feet in length, and the

result of the tenders was that two yards, one in the St. Lawrence area and one in the great lakes area, were the lowest tenderers for the three ships. The then minister of transport, the hon. member for Three Rivers, was dealing with this matter. I approached him at that time and said "If you want to get the work load shared around this country, why not give the lowest maritime yard a ship, one to the St. Lawrence and one to the great lakes?" That is what was done. One was launched in the St. Lawrence area and one in my area, at Pictou shipyards. I was not invited to the launching a short time ago, I do not know why. Nevertheless, the building of that ship created a lot of employment. That was one way in which we helped the Atlantic provinces.
Of course we do not pretend that during the six years we were in office we did everything which was required, but we got things moving along very well. I know that in 1950 or 1951 mines in my area began to close down, and at that time many of our younger people had nothing to turn to. It was then that a start should have been made in the provision of vocational training. That was done by the former government, and vocational schools have been built as a result of legislation which they brought in. One will be opened in my own area soon, and I am sure the Minister of Labour will be the first to admit that this is a step in the right direction to help our young people get the necessary technical training so they may make progress in their trades and stay in their own areas.
That is all I wish to say. My theme has been that although we may not have done everything in the last six years, we did start things rolling. Many of the ideas brought forward by the Minister of Labour and his colleagues are, in my view, only extensions of projects we commenced. We are very leery of the Minister of Finance, as all Canadians are. I hope to goodness the Minister of Labour is in thick with him as far as our native province is concerned, because we certainly need it.

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-72, to provide for the establishment of an economic council of Canada.
He said:
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, the measure now before us is, in my opinion, of vital importance. Its purpose is to establish economic planning in our country. That is why, before going over its main features, I should like first to try and explain that planning by giving a brief analysis of the economic problems we are faced with at the present time and to indicate exactly what kind of planning the government intends to adopt.
(Text):
The so-called inventory or short term cycle appears to be inherent in our present economic system. The mechanism of supply and demand is not self adjusting, at least over a short period of time. It would be surprising if it were, because it originates from the individual and free choice of millions of consumers and suppliers. The process of adjustment takes time, and it operates mainly through supply rather than demand factors. Demand remains fairly stable during the whole cycle, but as the upward phase develops supply increases more rapidly than demand. This inevitably leads to an involuntary accumulation of inventories which cannot go on indefinitely. When suppliers feel that inventories are too high they reduce new orders, thus bringing the transition between prosperity and recession; because, as a result, production and employment must decline. During the recession production increases more slowly or decreases more rapidly than demand, and suppliers draw on their inventories. This downward movement must come to an end 28902-5-133J
Economic Council of Canada before inventories are depleted and eventually new orders start to rise again. Thus conditions are set for a new phase of prosperity.
Inventory cycles have been fairly regular in Canada as elsewhere in peacetime. Each cycle, with its upward and downward movements, lasts for about three years. For instance, recessions have developed in 1954, 1957 and 1960; 1955, 1958 and 1961 have been years of recovery; 1956, 1959 and 1962 have been years of cyclical peaks. But even in the latter half of 1962 the Canadian economy was undergoing a considerable degree of hesitation and uncertainty. Total final demand levelled off in the third quarter of 1962, the first such pause since the low point of the last business cycle contraction.
We cannot hope to get rid of this important sources of economic instability without adequate planning arrangements, closer co-operation between the public and private sectors of the economy, and more flexible and selective policies.
But short term problems do not constitute the only difficulties we have to overcome. Indeed, several signs indicate that the Canadian economy since the late 1950's has been suffering from basic weaknesses and lack of growth, at a time when our labour force was and still is increasing rapidly. The gross national product per capita in constant dollars increased by 22 per cent between 1949 and 1956, but declined by about 4 per cent between 1956 and 1962. This is the most revealing sign of stagnation in Canada.
What seems to be the origin of that new trend? A rapid survey of the major components of our gross national product shows that consumer expenditures, exports and government expenditures have continued to grow and have contributed at the same time to growth. Investment is the only major component which has declined during that period. Between 1947 and 1957 total investment in constant dollars more than doubled, and increased each year except in 1954. Between 1957 and 1961 it had declined each year and the decrease reached about 13 per cent in 1961. During the same period investment in business capital as opposed to housing and social capital showed a reduction of approximately 25 per cent; yet expenditures on investment goods are precisely those which are the very immediate and basic cause of growth. What would be the essential reason, the main cause of this stagnation, of this inadequate growth?

speechtext:
As I was saying, Mr. Speaker, instead of engaging in a long explanation of that chronic anemia, I would simply like to give at this time an illustration of what seems to have happened in Canada in the last few years.
The paper and the automobile industries both owe their existence to technology which appeared in Canada, like in the rest of the world, at the turn of the century. At first, when they appeared on the scene, they represented a considerable potential of direct and indirect investment and employment.
We just have to think of the new plants, of the various power projects which have been carried out, of the lumber operations, of the development of the oil and steel industries, of the building of service stations and roads. Like many others which have contributed so much to our accelerated development, those industries will probably continue to expand in the future. But I think they will do so at a considerably slower pace, because, as I said a moment ago, they have practically finished developing their initial investment potential in the present context of world markets and traditional government policies.
If this diagnosis is correct, as I think it is, it should be a cause for worry, because it reveals a deep-seated ailment within our economy. That ailment cannot be healed by denouncing those who diagnose it as prophets of gloom and doom.
The problems created by recessions and stagnation in our country are made even more difficult today because of the upheavals in the world around us. Those upheavals, we find them first in the field of technology, where the first signs of a new technological revolution enable us to see already the rapid progress of automation which requires an ever more specialized labour force and which destroys, in its path, many of our traditional sources of employment.
Those upheavals, we find them also in the radical changes in the world trade patterns which take place under our eyes with the formation of huge trading blocs. Those upheavals will have deep repercussions on the Canadian economy and will require the radical transformation of several industries and regions.
It would be unrealistic to think that the private sector left to itself could overcome those difficulties. Radical changes presently taking place in the world and the adjustments

they will make necessary in our country, the recessions and the anemia affecting the Canadian economy demand not only a new association between the public and the private sectors, but also a bolder and more dynamic government leadership.
To overcome our present difficulties, we need new policies, applied in a new spirit and within new administrative structures. In other words, we need a plan so that the various aspects of the economic policy will be well co-ordinated and so that the private sector can work in the same direction as the government towards the common objective of harmonious growth.
That new role of the government is indicated to us by Pope John XXIII in Mater et Magistra, where he said:
It is requested of public authorities responsible for the common good, that they intervene in a wide variety of economic affairs, and that, in a more extensive and organized way ... It is necessary that they take active interest, the better to increase output of goods and to further social progress for the benefit of all citizens. This intervention of public authorities encourages, stimulates, regulates, supplements and complements.
It is easily seen that according to the Pope's thinking, the action of public authorities cannot be effective without planning. There is nothing too revolutionary in this, because to ignore planning is to leave human order to the determinism of chance. Any effective collective action needs a plan. Otherwise, you have anarchy, confusion and often failure, because to leave things to chance works only in particularly favourable circumstances. But the term planning itself is ambiguous and can mean two things quite different: indicative planning or imperative planning.
(Text):
In his book entitled "Beyond the Welfare State" Professor Myrdal underlines the fact that planning can take various forms. I want to quote him.
Economic planning is facing widely different problems for establishing goals, choosing means, fixing targets and implementing policies. Decisions on the public policies implied in planning are arrived at in very different ways and the sanctions applied in order to carry them into effect are also different.
Basically, planning can take two different forms. It can be a conscious and organized attempt by governments and other collective bodies to co-ordinate public and private policies more rationally in order to reach desirable economic objectives or goals more effectively. This is what is more and more called indicative planning, which provides
Economic Council of Canada wider knowledge of prospects and targets as well as credit and fiscal incentives, but which excludes compulsion and direct controls as normal instruments of state intervention. Planning can also be a systematic attempt by the state to impose economic goals on society and to use direct controls in order to achieve them. This is imperative planning which operates through compulsion.
Imperative planning provides a pattern which can be easily adapted to the conditions of underdeveloped countries. Here again I wish to quote Professor Myrdal.
By the very logic of the underdeveloped countries' situation, planning becomes programmatic in its approach. It does not, as in the western countries, force itself upon a national community through a gradual process which finally results in a fait accompli... In the underdeveloped countries the idea precedes its realization. As economic development cannot be expected to come by itself, planning becomes a precondition for development, not, as in the western countries, a later consequence of development and all the other changes which accompanied it. . . (In the underdeveloped countries), in principle and in theory, planning anticipates public policies. It does not grow out of the necessity to co-ordinate such policies as have already been initiated.
It would be very surprising if indicative planning could succeed in the underdeveloped countries because they do not have the infrastructure of voluntary organizations which that kind of planning requires. It would perhaps be even more surprising if imperative planning could work in the democratic and industrialized countries of the western world.
In Canada, for instance, we have developed a mixed economy with a public and a private sector. Consumers, private producers and labour unions cherish their freedom. Public authorities can influence their behaviour but they could not control their decisions, certainly not in peacetime. Direct and permanent controls on investment, production, prices and wages, which are required by - imperative planning in a mixed economy, would not only be politically unacceptable but would also give very poor economic results. Private investment, for instance, is a highly volatile phenomenon and does not respond positively to compulsion.
Imperative planning would prove to be unworkable at the national level in Canada for another obvious reason. The federal government does not have the constitutional powers required to impose direct control and it is very unlikely that it would succeed in getting such powers which fall under provincial jurisdiction at the present time.
Thus, in a country like Canada, imperative planning would be politically unacceptable, economically undesirable and constitutionally unworkable.

The planning which the government advocates and intends to initiate is essentially indicative and incentive planning. It will be a planning without any coercion and control. In our opinion, this is the only kind of planning desirable and feasible in our country.
I have no intention, at this stage, to explain in detail the bill under study. Its purpose is to establish an economic council which will consist of a chairman, two directors and 25 other members. This council will have three main duties. First of all, it will have to initiate research on all aspects of our economic life, try to foresee the normal behaviour of the economy and define the rate of growth, on the whole and by sectors, which is needed for the full use of our resources. In other words, the economic council will have to prepare a plan.
The council will also submit recommendations to the government on policies to be followed and on the means of promoting the highest possible level of employment and production in our country. It will therefore have the responsibility of recommending methods and processes capable of insuring the implementing of the plan.
The council will finally take over the functions heretofore given to the national productivity council. That integration, in the opinion of all the interested parties, has become most desirable and does not imply in any way that this government is lacking confidence in the members of the national productivity council. On the contrary, I wish on behalf of the government, to express to Mr. DeYoung and all the members of the council our most sincere appreciation for the services they have rendered. I am sure that the experience they acquired and the work they have done will be most profitable to the new economic council.
So, the purpose of this bill is to institute economic planning in Canada through a close consultation with the provinces and the private sector of our economy. For that purpose, it provides for the establishment of an economic council with very wide responsibilities in the field of research and very vast powers of recommendation. It creates planning structures both wide and flexible. Thus, we shall be in a much better position than

before not only for acquiring a true knowledge of our economic problems but also, I hope, to find practical solutions.

Order. I have certain remarks on the admissibility of this bill which I would like to give the house now. The purpose of this bill is to delete from the general powers of railway companies the power to "alienate, sell or dispose of, any lands or property of the company that for any reason have become not necessary for the purpose of the railway". In other words, according to the explanatory note:
The purpose ... is to emphasize ... that abandoned railway lands and the property thereon are royalties accruing to the public and not to the railway company's shareholders.

According to section 16 of the Canadian National Railways Act, chapter 29 of the statutes of 1955, the provisions of the Railway Act apply to the national company. There is no doubt that if this amendment were adopted it would prejudicially affect the assets and revenues of Canadian National Railways. Furthermore it would increase the annual deficit of the Canadian National Railways for which parliament has to provide.
For the above reasons it is a money bill and cannot be introduced by a private member, according to the provisions of the British North America Act and of the standing orders of the house. On May 9, 1933 it was decided by Mr. Speaker Black that an amendment involving an expenditure to be incurred by the Canadian National Railways is out of order because the railway is owned by the government. See Beauchesne's third edition, page 497. Mr. Speaker ruled the proposed amendment out of order on the grounds that it involved an expenditure of public moneys and could only be moved by a minister on the recommendation of the crown. From this ruling there was an appeal, and the question being put: Shall the ruling of the Chair be sustained; it was decided in the affirmative.
Accordingly, I believe this bill to be in the nature of a money bill and I declare it to be out of order.

I refer to the opinion of the deputy minister of justice which is set out in the explanatory notes to the bill.

The setting up of a position similar to that occupied by an ombudsman, as he is known in the Scandinavian countries, will be welcomed by a large section of the public. I should like to speak on this point of order and particularly with reference to the remark made by the hon. member for Greenwood. He has referred to citation 366 of Beauchesne's fourth edition. I should like to go further and refer the house to the ruling of Mr. Speaker Casgrain referred to in that paragraph. The bill in question was one similar to the bill the admissibility of which we are now discussing. The mover of this bill proposes that a certain official or officials of one department should be transferred to another post. The ruling of the Speaker on this earlier occasion might be summarized under two headings: first, whether or not existing staff continuing to be used in the service, but being shifted to an additional function would, as a practical necessity, require the expenditure of additional public funds, it being understood that where extra funds are needed parliament should specifically provide for them. The second ground on which the Speaker of that day ruled against the bill could most expeditiously be put forward by reading from the ruling itself. I am reading from the House of Commons Journals for Friday, February 21, 1936 at page 62:
Another element which places this measure in the category of money bills is that its adoption would mean the transfer of the authority under which appropriated money is to be spent. The translators' salaries have been voted as part of the estimates of the Secretary of State's department. This was done by resolution in committee of supply and it was subsequently embodied in the appropriation bill. When money is voted, the main conditions imposed on its expenditure are embodied in resolutions. All the circumstances concerning its destination form part of the appropriation with which they are considered and if any alteration is to be made it must be by the same process as the original resolution.
A money bill is defined in the British house as a public bill which contains only provisions dealing with inter alia the "custody" of public money. The custody is undoubtedly the placing of an appropriation under a certain minister.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I maintain that what the hon. member for Red Deer is proposing is that the expenditure which has been authorized under the Department of Justice should be transferred out of that department and be dealt with in accordance with the appropriation resolutions concerning the House of Commons, and that would be contrary to the ruling of Mr. Speaker Casgrain.

For that reason, I submit that Your Honour should rule against the propriety of this bill.

On the order for the second reading of a somewhat similar bill, namely a bill to establish the office of parliamentary proctor, etc.; on April 6, 1962, Mr. Speaker Michener said, among other things, as reported on page 2597 of Hansard:
Before calling on the hon. member or recognizing the hon. member, may I say that I feel it to be my duty to draw the attention of the house to the fact that this bill has some of the characteristics of a money bill, or one that requires a resolution. I therefore feel that if the debate proceeds I should at least indicate the possible difficulties with a bill of this kind so that it will not be taken as a firm precedent for similar legislation.
It is true that the present bill is somewhat different, more particularly in that it does not provide directly for the payment of a salary for the parliamentary commissioner or his staff. On the contrary it states in clause 3 that:
The parliamentary commissioner shall be chosen among the senior law officers of the Department of Justice-
-etc. As to the staff, clause 6 is to the effect that:
The parliamentary commissioner may from time to time obtain the services of such officers and employees of the Senate, the House of Commons and the Department of Justice-

From this it may be deducted, first, that there will be transfers from one department to the other; second, that it is quite probable that the officers so appointed will have to be replaced by others; and third, that a new office or branch will be created.
I am of the opinion that this bill is a money bill and for that reason it cannot be introduced by a private member. It is inconceivable that the numerous duties of parliamentary commissioner as suggested in the bill could be assumed without an expenditure of money. The officers transferred from other departments will have to be paid, probably at an increased rate of pay. They will have to be replaced in the departments from which they have been transferred by new employees, thus creating a number of new employees.

Another element which places this measure in the category of money bills is that its adoption would mean the transfer of the authority under which appropriated money is to be spent.
And further:
When money is voted, the main conditions imposed on its expenditure are embodied in resolutions. All the circumstances concerning its destination form a part of the appropriation with which they are considered and if any alteration is to be made it must be by the same process as the original resolution.
And still further:
-the circumstances under which an expenditure is to be made are indivisible from that expenditure.
