He believes that such a board if set up could put an inefficient and irresponsible government, as he says, on the spot. I make no observation on that; I do not know whether they have set up that committee yet.
With regard to private enterprise, he concludes from what is happening that it needs direction. This is my conclusion from reading what he says. He says that production is being misdirected by private enterprise, which may rely on advertising to create its market, which may concentrate the public attention on low priority wants when it should be interested in other things, and which may neglect other important objectives. This is the philosophy, sir. "He who runs may read". This is the philosophy behind the planning upon which this government has embarked. He says that Canada should develop its secondary industry, and certainly it should. Then he goes on to say that this should not be done by encouraging small manufacturing behind a wall of protection; that such industry should engage in competition on a wider scale. Then he says this of a government interested in small business:
This may involve a smaller number of larger units in each industry.
What happens to small business? What happens to the little business places in all of our towns and cities?
Then he goes on to deal with the north, because he covers everything. He deals with the opening up of the north. He does not rely much on developing the north. While the Canadian north will undoubtedly play an important role in the Canadian economy, he says, the huge private and public investment required to open up this vast economic frontier will make a much greater contribution to general welfare if it is used for the time being in the more settled parts of the country. This, sir, is the philosophy. He goes on to say that in order to keep prices properly in line under the selective fiscal policies which


are advocated, business and agriculture should meet at an annual conference at which objectives would be explained and the sense of social responsibility developed to discourage conflicts, such as labour pressure for higher wages, when such increases are not in the public interest.
This, Mr. Speaker, is an amazing document: it is frank, comprehensive and far-seeing, from the point of view of the hon. gentleman who wrote it. He says that we should learn to use new tools of economic policy. From a reading, even a perusal, of the two documents to which I refer, hon. members of this house will get an understanding of the philosophy which activates this government.
This measure cannot be considered in isolation; it is one of a great panorama planned for three long years in every detail. This measure must be viewed in the light of the other measures which have been introduced. The declaration of purpose is to stimulate the economy in order to provide jobs, and there are elements in it which are deserving of the widest possible support, for anything that can be done in that direction deserves the consideration and approval of parliament. But I find it difficult to understand the objective in question alongside the tax on building materials and new machinery. One naturally wonders how much of the economy will be left to stimulate, by the time some of these other measures start to function. The council will be set up and asked to do its work on the basis of a budget that is all but vanished, with some parts of the rest of it unworkable or meaningless. This measure cannot be separated from the other measures, for they create the atmosphere in which the national economic council is being set up. By way of example, what manner of thinking brought about the suggestion of a $500 bonus on winter-built homes? When it was announced, every person owning a home in Canada had in effect $500 less value for his own home and had to provide the taxes so that someone else could get $500. What an army of inspectors it is going to take to go out in December to inspect the sites and to go out in March to see whether or not the conditions have been fulfilled. It will provide a nightmare of bureaucratic confusion. What about the plan to pay one half the salary up to $150 per month of workers over 45 years of age who are hired? It puts a limitation on wages for everyone. The planners planned, but they did not think ahead. All of this, as I say, is part of the same picture.
The municipal loan fund was launched with tremendous fanfare. We do not know where it is. Questions were asked today. It is going to come up. It went off in the blue. We have

not heard much of it since. It was sighted over Quebec yesterday. That is all we know about it. In fact, it was sighted in the Quebec legislature just this morning when the premier of Quebec termed this legislation a breach of promise by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson). Is that legislation still in orbit, because it is part and parcel of this economic planning?
With respect to the legislation before us to set up a board with similar powers to those provided in Bill No. C-87 introduced last November, we give it our support. In part it is a duplication of that bill. I make it clear that in so far as it consists of a duplication of that bill and of the National Productivity Council Act we naturally give it support. But it has other things in it, and I am only going to point out one on this occasion. It has in it a provision that indicates how the budget is interlocked with the establishment of an economic council for Canada. The clause is an omnibus one, and it has to do with the fostering of plans for economic development by way of studying means of increasing Canadian participation in the ownership, control and management of industries in Canada.
The government have determined on the course. They made a frightful mess of their planning in this connection. The 30 per cent tax went with the birds and the truth squad. The other day there was a further change, and yet in the face of the planning that has been done provision is made in this bill that the board is to study means of increasing Canadian participation. I suggest that when they set up a board for this purpose, among other things, they have determined on the course they are going to take before it is set up. The board is also to study the potentialities of growth and the like, and to explore and evaluate particular projects of major significance. Those are desirable objectives and with those objectives we are in agreement.
However, sir, in this legislation there are quite a number of clauses that invade provincial jurisdiction and constitute an interference with the constitutional rights of the provinces. All during the election campaign and prior thereto it was said that before the municipal loans plan was brought in the provinces would be consulted. That was the undertaking. When the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr) was Minister of Labour he brought in the winter works program. He received widespread support for it because he consulted with the other levels of government before bringing it in.
Within the ambit of the bill now before us there are various elements of intrusion into the provincial arena, and I think there should have been consultation. I know it has been suggested that after some of this legislation
Economic Council of Canada has been passed by parliament the provinces are going to be consulted. That is not consultation. Consultation consists in taking the counsel of these various levels of government before legislation is passed.
Indeed, I think we should endeavour to bring about in our federal-provincial relations new vistas of consultation. During the period that the government of which I had the honour to be the head was in office we brought about a system. I do not say it was perfect but it was a workable solution to many of the problems of a federal state. I think we will have to establish something in the nature of a general course of conduct so that we will not forever be fighting the battles of federal-provincial jurisdiction and the like. We did that in connection with the resource ministers council. The hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) convened a conference on the subject of resources for tomorrow. Out of that conference came the resource ministers council. During the discussions and consultations a minister from each of the provinces took part in a study of what each province was doing, and a program was worked out which could be recommended to all the governments. It provided for a secretariat which is responsible to no one government, but to a committee set up by the resource ministers themselves.
The hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey) has a resolution on the order paper, and while I am not saying I agree with it in its entirety it does have elements in it that are necessary to be imparted into any arrangements to assure continuing consultation with the provinces.
As a result of the resource ministers council being formed they have worked out problems in co-operation. They have been able to bring about agreement. The president of the council at the present time is the Hon. Rene Levesque. The presidency changes regularly. As we are trying to make the constitution more workable and more effective, all of which is dependant on consultation, I think we have to work out under our system a general plan of operation. The technique that we evolved was not, as I said, perfect. It was the result of trial, error and experiment, but I think we evolved a system whereby federal concepts make possible co-operative planning of admirable programs in all fields, as has been done in the resource field. We did that too in the Department of Agriculture, under the Agricultural Rehabilitation and Development Act.
I mention this as an aside, and as a digression, that we must do all we can to set up some form of flexible machinery which will permit the functioning of full co-operation and consultation between the federal and provincial governments. I am concerned over

Economic Council of Canada what is happening in connection with the municipal loan fund. The spirit of co-operation that was built up between the two levels of government by the means I have already mentioned has been seriously diminished in consequence of the action of the present government in proceeding with legislation, however admirable, without the fullest consultation and consideration.
Having said that, sir, I want to point out that except for one or two particulars to which I have alluded, the principle in general that is followed here is in no way new. We had it in our legislation, in the bill to which I have already referred, to establish a national economic development board. The Liberal party, in the House of Commons, said it agreed with the plan, and then proceeded for seven days to talk about it. We spent two days on the resolution stage and five days on second reading and in committee of the whole. Finally, with dissolution, it ended. They said they believed in the principles. They accepted our idea for directional planning without coercion or compulsion, and unaccompanied by the philosophy of coercion that seems to be characteristic of this government. At the same time, they opposed the measure day after day.
It is very interesting to look back and to find that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) said they agreed with what was being done. The present Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) agreed in general with it, and then proceeded to advance many arguments to show that it would not be operative. At page 819 of Hansard, for October 22, 1962 he uttered these immortal words:
We need a government which is not afraid of taking positive action; a government which knows what it would do.
They took action, all right, under their budgetary plans; then in panic they threw them overboard, not all at once but one by one. They referred to a government which knew what it would do. But what is more important is a government which knows what it wants to do and, having decided it, stays with it. We do not know what the next step is. We have not got the legislation. I believe there are many people across Canada who, in view of the representations being made now, expect a few more of the principles which were the cornerstones of the new economy building in this country will be thrown overboard between now and the enactment of legislation.
The creation of a national economic development council, as I said a moment ago, is not new. We provided for that, and we provided for a national productivity council. However, when the present Minister of Finance was speaking, he contended that what we were doing in that legislation was setting


up a board which would emasculate the national productivity council. This was the criticism he made last fall. Now, they are throwing the national productivity council overboard by placing at least some of its principles with this board.
In the United Kingdom, sir, an economic council was set up. I am not going into the particulars of it. However, I would point out that several reports have been made by the British national economic development council and they are well worth reading. One is a study of the growth rate in the United Kingdom economy to 1966, and it was published in April of this year. This is the type of planning to which no one can object. It is unaccompanied by the philosophy that planning is an end in itself, that the planners have some superior source of information or inspiration above ordinary human beings and they will tell you where you should go; that they know what is good for you. We have had enough of that kind of planning in the budget. The planning provided for under the national economic development council in the United Kingdom was on the basis that the economic growth rate, which was 2.2 per cent per year, should be increased to a growth rate of 4 per cent where possible by 1966.
They said the United Kingdom has ample scientific trained personnel; that industry will have to be more efficient. As the hon. gentleman said this afternoon there must be a heavier and more rapid investment in industrial capacity. The report from the United Kingdom deals with the deficit in the balance of payments, and indicates that exports will have to be increased sharply; consumer expenditures will have to be increased substantially; that government, management and trade unions will have to co-operate closely to achieve an annual increase in growth rate. Then, there is a further report that came out on June 6, "Conditions Favourable to Faster Growth".
In so far as the present bill is a counterpart of that which we introduced, and which was talked out, it receives our full and complete support. I mentioned a moment ago that I could not understand the incorporation in this bill of the provision that a study is to be made for increasing Canadian participation. Why did they not wait until they had recommendations? Why set up a national economic council, with a major portion of its power being this, and then act in advance? I think it can be said now that this is the kind of advice that may have saved the government from the perpetration of the terrible errors that characterized its earlier resolution in this regard.

In so far as the bill is concerned, when compared with the bill we introduced, we find that the bill we introduced provided for study and report. It would have co-operated with regional agencies in the field of economic study and planning. The present bill deletes the words "study and report", and substitutes "advise and recommend." The present board would have powers to promote and organize in order to secure economic growth, and will carry on its programs until they can be transferred to other departments or agencies. In so far as those powers are concerned, they come perilously close to the centralized planning backed by the power to compel and direct.
In reading this bill in its entirety, taking the whole picture envisaged in its concept, one can only conclude this: Whatever the minister said and however definitely and frankly he suggests that there will be no coercion, this board is designed plainly as an agency to promote a planners' paradise for the Canadian economy. It is skillfully worded. The hon. gentleman smiles. That was his philosophy in 1960; that was his philosophy when he wrote the book. However, Mr. Speaker, experience is a great teacher and it may well be that in the light of even the experience of the last three months the hon. gentleman has learned that theory is often difficult to translate into effective action.
I have mentioned the attitude of the opposition last fall. They said they accepted the bill and then proceeded to dissect it. They argued; they postponed, and discussion went on from day to day. We do not intend to do that. In so far as the bill is concerned in having the objectives of the bill that we placed before parliament, it will receive our full support, but when we come to deal with some of the paragraphs and clauses we shall point out their effect and endeavour to bring about a change.
As to the portion that is actually a prototype of the powers of the National Productivity Council Act, it will receive our support, although I feel free to say that bringing together production, automation and productivity all under one board is going to be very difficult. Our attitude will be to do everything we can to make the bill effective in its operation while assuring the supremacy of parliament in the decisions that are made by the board, while maintaining the constitutional rights of the provinces strictly and absolutely, and while at the same time being entirely opposed to anything in the nature of a planned economy, however estimable the planners may be.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND DEFINITION OF DUTIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my intention to come directly to the bill before us which is concerned with setting up an economic council of Canada.
Economic Council of Canada In principle such an economic council is sound and it can serve a useful purpose. If it is set up properly it can be an effective instrument in reducing the severe tension existing among labour, management and government. However its success will depend largely on its terms of reference, and for this reason our debate at this time is most important.
There should be a national economic council to assist in maintaining the efficiency of the economy. I believe this is its basic purpose, and as such it must be an advisory group and not a policy making body.
Boards and councils are no panacea. As I read through this proposed legislation I can see that there is a possibility of real conflict with the work of the Atlantic development board. There are also some important points of similarity to last year's legislation which died on the order paper, and which we should examine closely.
Reading from an editorial in the Globe and Mail of June 11, 1963, written by Bruce Macdonald I find this:
Like the economic development board, the economic council is directed to make to the minister an annual report, which is to be tabled in parliament. Unlike the board, the council has no authority to publish certain special studies without the consent of the minister.
This is an important point which the article makes, and it goes on to say:
The only new feature in the bill relating to this question is laid down in these words: "The council shall, annually, prepare and cause to be published a review of medium and long term prospects and
problems."
While this may well be subject to interpretation, the council could well consider its freedom is sharply circumscribed by the lengthy list of subjects on which it is directed to report only to the government.
I believe a tone is indicated in this legislation which is dangerous, if the national economic council is to perform the functions which are urgently required at this time.
In many respects this bill overlaps and is similar to the legislation which set up the national productivity council and it, by the way, is being repealed by this bill, with the exception that there is a tendency to keep the control of the economic council in the hands of the government. This is not the type of thing which is needed if we are to assure ourselves that there will be that spirit of co-operation among labour, management and government which is necessary if the council is to accomplish its purpose.
There has been an aspect of the work of the national productivity council over the last couple of years which I believe is noteworthy, and which should be carried through in this legislation if the new economic council is to be of any real use.

Economic Council oj Canada
The national productivity council has taken the lead in setting up, or assisting in the setting up of provincial and local councils. This is an aspect of its work which is very important. If the new council is to replace the national productivity council then we must make note of this feature.
Reading from the report of an address made by H. George DeYoung, chairman of the national productivity council at the fourth national labour-management seminar at the University of Montreal on May 15, I find this:
From our very beginning it was also readily apparent to the council that the establishment of provincial and local councils was a necessity if our goal of aiding the economy by improving its competitive ability were to be effective. Because Canada is Canada, no Ottawa based group will ever solve problems in the various provinces unilaterally.
The problems are different, the people are more geographically oriented than nationally and our type of work must eventually be done on the job, in factory and office, and on the farm. While we have been working to remove the fundamental roadblocks on a national scale-those imposed by law- of statistic and measurement data lack, and the greatest one of the climate for labour-management-government co-operation, we have been building toward the time when the local council would be the headliner. Steps were undertaken quickly to review with the provincial governments and representatives of labour and management the need for such provincial organizations. We found, interestingly that Quebec was already moving and Indeed ahead of the rest of Canada in this aspect of forming a broadly based economic council. Action is also now under way to set up local councils in many industrial cities.
The formation of these productivity or economic councils in the provinces across Canada is proceeding well. Already, full formed councils are operational in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Quebec, Ontario and Saskatchewan-
And, since these words were spoken, in Alberta.
-while organizational efforts are at reasonably advanced stages in most of the other provinces. The success in the maritimes was advanced by the work of the Atlantic provinces economic council and is now highlighted by the signing of a management-labour manifesto of co-operation.
This quotation from the chairman of the national productivity council brings home to us the lesson that if the national economic council is to achieve its objectives it must not be too tightly controlled by the national government. It must extend its responsibility outward to both labour and management and to the provinces and the local areas as well. Otherwise we will have a repetition of the very thing which is happening now with regard to the municipal development and loan board. Here the central government has laid out the specifications and qualifications concerning the assistance which this particular legislation is meant to provide, but has run afoul of local autonomy and the local good will which is necessary if this project is to


succeed. The lesson brought home to us here is simply that the whole question of planning and of industrial development must be coordinated in order to prevent the economy from rushing off madly in all directions.
The planning that industry and business needs is orderly and practical encouragement to expand. In principle a businessman can plan better for himself than can a bureaucrat in Ottawa acting on his behalf. Federal responsibilities include the co-ordinating aspect based on principles which have just been enunciated and which will encourage provincial responsibility and respect of provincial autonomy and rights while at the same time bringing about the federal-provincial co-operation we must have if such a council as this is to succeed. No one would want to take power or authority away from the government. What we want to do here is to add the wisdom of the economic community to that of the government in the decision-making process.
This brings us to consultant government, and this is one of the reasons why the recent budget has resulted in failure-simply because there was not that consultation with, or consideration of, those to whom the legislation would apply. We have seen the results and this should bring home the important principle I am talking about.
The other day I came across a booklet which is a digest of the report of the labour-management-government mission to Europe sponsored by the national productivity council. On page 9, I read this:
At the national level the consultative function in economic development is carried out through joint councils or bodies whose members, particularly from labour and management, represent the major interest involved in the economic life of the country. They make recommendations concerning common objectives of economic and social policy and the means for achieving the agreed objectives. They have not only a voice in the formulation of government economic and social policy but they must share some responsibility for its successful implementation.
I see in this piece of legislation a number of danger points. I shall not go over them in detail at this time because we are talking about the general principle of the bill, but they must be gone over carefully point by point when we come to the committee stage of our discussions. In this regard I should like to refer to a speech by Mr. J. Claude Hebert made in Halifax a short time ago entitled, "How Labour, Management and Government in Europe have United for Economic Growth". In the course of the speech to the Nova Scotia branch of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, Mr. Hebert said this:
I am also convinced, as I have said, of the need for consultative bodies at national, provincial and

local levels. The national productivity council was a good start. It should be expanded or a larger body formed which unites with the council to conduct national economic studies with full consultation between labour, management and government. This is what is proving so highly effective in Europe. Such studies must also be repeated at provincial level and we now see a number of provinces developing economic councils.
Representatives of employer organizations and representatives of official trade unions must sit together along with government, finance and other groups to study the problems hindering economic growth. I say this because I am convinced that the running of our economy is too important to be left to governments alone or to political parties. Management and labour must be brought in on national and provincial policy making. It is too easy for a government, or a department of government, to become a world unto itself. They are not to blame,-it is just human nature. It happens in companies where a special department can become isolated from the real needs of a company. Many of you may have experienced this. We must bring all those involved in the economy into consultation before basic decisions are made which affect our business life.
Because this is the principle which has been followed in countries such as Sweden, West Germany, The Netherlands, Belgium and Great Britain, we see that councils similar to that proposed in this piece of legislation have achieved effective and desirable results-something we have not yet achieved in this country. This is probably one of the basic reasons why we are faced with our present difficulties.
The leader of the official opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) has been speaking about the tremendous expansion of growth that took place last year. We must consider in this the increase in prices, and other factors which do not represent true economic growth, and average the position out over the last four or five years. If hon. members do that they will find an entirely different picture-not even enough progress to keep up with the expanding population and rising prices. For this reason the terms of reference of this new body are extremely important.
I wish to make a few closing remarks which summarize the basic principles involved in such legislation as this, if it is to reach the objective which hon. members hope it will attain. First I believe this council must be truly consultative in its functions. This means that labour, management, and all other aspects of our economy must be consulted at the decision making stage by the government in order that the government can decide on the right policy to take. Second then, as far as possible, the council must be able to act apart from politics. Since it is designed to work with both management and labour, as well as with government; since it is intended to co-operate with provincial governments and local councils, it is important that it should have complete freedom to make its
Economic Council of Canada findings known. In this legislation there are several points which appear to me to be restrictive in this regard because the responsibility of this council is not to the government alone but to the economy in general. Third, we must recognize that during the last two years there has been a tremendous amount of sound, solid work done by the national productivity council. This must be taken into account and used and incorporated into the work of the council we are now discussing. The national productivity council has played an important part in changing the class war in industry to a situation of co-operation between industry and labour. This is something which we as politicians, finding ourselves enclosed by these walls for far too much of the time, do not properly understand. I think that in the last few years there has been a much higher degree of cooperation, good will, and productive planning between labour and industry than we have ever had before. We should give the national productivity council a good deal of the credit for this, as it has brought the different aspects of our economy together.
Then, last, a further point I wish to make concerns research. We in Canada have perhaps not been sufficiently concerned about the importance of research as it applies to industry and, indeed, to all aspects of our economy. It is necessary that work on such programs be continued and expanded.
Another aspect of this bill which has disturbed me is to be found in the latter part of the legislation and it concerns finance. I find that the minister places the responsibility for financing the national economic council more or less in the hands of the government alone. I wonder how many of us here, including members of the government, know how much money has been spent in the last year by the national productivity council. I find that for the last fiscal year it amounted to $400,894. Where did this come from? One hundred and fifty thousand dollars came from the statutory allotment provided for the council. One hundred thousand dollars or so was carried over from the previous year when the council was just getting going and did not spend the whole of its allotment. About $86,000 came to the council as donations from industry and labour. This is the kind of co-operation we need. Nevertheless the present legislation is preventing the development of a situation of this type. Finally, $83,000 of the council's income came from matching grants. There are, it is true, a few other miscellaneous sources of income which go to make up the total; but what is important here is the spirit of co-operation which these accounts reflect. Yet this bill

Economic Council of Canada actually eliminates the possibility of the kind of contribution which, in my view, is so necessary if this spirit of co-operation is to develop as it should.
It is therefore of great importance that the work of this economic council should be carried out on a continuing basis in collaboration with management and labour and other programs rather than that it should just evolve into a civil service operation. Good as such an operation might be, it would inevitably achieve only part of the end desired and certainly remove it far from its real objective.
This new council could be a sounding board for assessing how effectively other government programs operate or, indeed, a standard of comparison by which the programs of other governments such as provincial or local governments, in meeting the real needs which industry and labour encounter in their daily work can be assessed. Therefore, we give our wholehearted support to this legislation. There are weaknesses contained in it, but these can be discussed when we come to speak about the specific clauses involved. In principle this council has something which the economy of Canada needs- this is particularly true of the work that has been done by the national productivity council-provided it can be expanded and extended, as it needs to be at this time, and provided the basic principles to which I have referred are made the motivating force behind the council and its functions.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND DEFINITION OF DUTIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, following the previous speaker, who seemed to be above politics, I am going to try to get down to politics. This bill is-I know the minister who brought it in will forgive me for using a bit of a theological metaphor-hardly the bell, book and candle of the New Democratic party. But I notice he did give the blessing to this through a quotation from one of the letters of Pope John, in a religious sense. The New Democratic party economic theology has long dealt with, and our predecessors have certainly dealt with the idea of an economic council. The fact that this particular council is hardly, in its framework as specific in its responsibilities is no reason for our being destructive regarding it. We support the bill and we shall vote for it; but we are not hotly enthusiastic about it: you might say we are lukewarm.
I would like to say that with regard to the speech of the Leader of the Opposition I was almost bitterly disappointed in that, given the points that he made about the difficulties today, in any planning terms, in the need for provincial consultation; given the fact that he can point with a certain amount

of derision to Premier Lesage and the municipal development loan fund; given the fact he can point to that great economist, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) and what has happened to him, with all those experts he brought in, the fact remains that the attempt the Leader of the Opposition seems to be involved in, is to somehow limn or detail the Liberal party, the present government, as being dedicated to some kind of bureaucratic planning that is going to menace the freedoms of this nation. This is a little bit too much to swallow. I am not saying this in defence of the government, but somehow we get almost the spectre that we have a Barry Goldwater or a Pat Walsh added to development in thinking on the part of the official opposition with regard to this kind of legislation, and this is really pushing it a bit far.
I would like to point out to the Leader of the Opposition that he introduced some legislation that some of us, if we wanted to raise this particular kind of ghosts, could get quite excited and worried about. I think the Conservative government, if it has any legislative legacy that a historian a decade or two from now will be looking back and trying to gild a bit, it will probably be ARDA. Can you think of any more general measure that has ever been brought here to give more power and planning and spending authority, which is almost removed from parliament? It is a good piece of legislation, and I think it is developing very nicely. So that the leader of a party so proud of that piece of legislation and the good effects it promises to have, and has already had, raising this terrible spectre of this bureaucratic menace across the way, is hard to take.
The Leader of the Opposition comes from the prairies where more than a generation ago the farmers became fed up with the whole play of the free market and free prices in terms of the grain trade. So they organized through political pressure a move which led to the taking away of wheat from any free market. There is nothing more planned and controlled, as is evidenced by the questions which roll from this side of the house from our prairie friends, than the whole grain market in the west; and for their leader, given that kind of background, to start worrying about economic planning at this date is incomprehensible to me.
I can give an example from the former prime minister's own program where some kind of economic analysis should appeal to him. The Conservative party is very proud of the Technical and Vocational Training Assistance Act which was passed a couple of years ago. This act has pumped millions of dollars into new construction, and one of the great arguments put forward by my Conservative

friends is that it gave a boost to the economy last year and things improved. When the minister of labour brought that legislation in he gave us an estimate of how much would be spent by the government on this project in ten years, and his economic analysis was so good that the federal government wound up, before the Conservatives went out of power, committing themselves in two and a half years to as much as they projected spending in ten years.
Some people may say that this shows what a wonderful measure it was, but surely it also shows how terribly badly off we are in terms of economic analysis. I was told the other day that the head of the economic research bureau of the Department of Labour happens to be a chartered accountant, and remembering what recently happened to another chartered accountant here, maybe that is the explanation for that poor analysis.
I should like to suggest that there is another way in which we can look at this economic council without raising all these terrible fears that this is a bureaucratic menace. The Glassco report-I know hon. members on the Conservative side have a certain amount of interest and even pride in this-in volume 3, in the section dealing with economic services, points out that the current level of expenditures can be described as modest, probably unduly so. That is referring to the economic analyses and the statistical services available to the federal government at the present time. The report goes on, in commenting on D.B.S.:
The highly concentrated organization of statistical operations of the public service reflects a deliberate policy decision, taken 45 years ago, to create a centralized statistical agency, the dominion bureau of statistics. In contrast-
-and this is the point I want to make- no specific policy has been enunciated with respect to economic analysis which developed, into an organized activity employing substantial staffs only during world war II.
Then the report goes on to indicate that at the present time economic analysis is concentrated largely in three places-the Department of Trade and Commerce, the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Labour. Surprisingly enough, the conclusion drawn by the Glassco commission is that the Department of Finance itself, which might be considered the key department, is remarkably short of people who can do economic analysis.
Under economic intelligence the Glassco report says:
Some economists, perhaps best exemplified by those in the Bank of Canada and the departments of finance and trade and commerce, are engaged in general economic intelligence; they are constantly observing economic trends and develop-
Economic Council of Canada ments, both national and international, which may have widespread significance for the whole Canadian economy.
Then it goes on to point out that in all these stages of working environments for economic analysts and statisticians there has been no great emphasis on economists and economic analysts in the federal civil service. There is no real need to fear the creation of a few more economists. The working environment, according to the Glassco report, contains this kind of situation:
-in some departments senior administrators have only a cloudy conception of economic analysis, which usually results in an attitude of naive skepticism toward economics in general. The mere engagement of a number of economists is not particularly productive, if senior officials do not understand how these professionals can contribute to the work of the department.
This is a point I want to draw to the attention of the government in view of some of the later suggestions which I wish to make. The commissioner said:
Your commissioners are satisfied that, having regard to the widely dispersed and varied needs for economic analysis in the public service, it would be impracticable to establish a central economic bureau which would1 second economists to departments and agencies in need of their services.
However, the personnel division of the treasury board should maintain an active and continuous interest in the development of career opportunities for economists, as for other professional public servants.
And the report goes on to say how that can be done.
Then in order to make its point with regard to economic analysis, the Glassco commission went to the trouble of analysing the French, the British and the American experience. Since there seemed to be some more parallels between the U.S. president's council of economic advisers and this council which we have here, it might be worth while, I think, to make a few references to the president's council of economic advisers. The council publishes every year a report which goes to the president, and is associated with his report to congress on the economic state of the union. The intriguing thing about the economic council of advisers is its very wide acceptance on the American scene. I suppose it is really only a few people, like those in the John Birch society or Barry Goldwater, who worry about the council of economic advisers.
One of the former members of this council, Neil Jacoby, who was an academic economist working out of a California university, has made a number of points in connection with this council of economic advisers to which I should like to draw the attention of the minister. The minister has the problem of having 25 occasional members of the

Economic Council of Canada board, if you want to put it that way, and three full time members. I think our experience with the board of broadcast governors and the C.B.C. indicates that having a trio of full time people and a congregation of so called interested parties across the country really has not worked very well, at least if we believe all the stories we have heard recently about the dichotomy of interests between the permanent members, who are the experts, and these occasional people who come in. In the United States the council of economic advisers is not saddled with a bunch of people who pretend to be representative. What you have is a chairman and two advisers. These three people have been in every case academicians, or academic economists. Or if you want to put it a little more broadly, they are people who are trained in economics and know something about it. I cannot think of anything more fatuous in some ways than to appoint three full-time people to this Canadian job who are not economists. You have men like George DeYoung, for example, who is not trained in economics and who obviously- here I differ very markedly with the leader of the Social Credit party-has been going around the country speaking to Rotary and chamber of commerce banquets and whipping up exhortations about the beauties of labour-management co-operation. He and the national productivity council never did get down to any real outline of our problems in the productivity area and they did not come up with a single economic study that will bear any kind of test of time except, I suppose, for the report on the trip to Europe which was the casually interesting sort of fact finding tour that had been made long ago by some of our academic and professional economists. The news that they brought back was only surprising, I suppose, to those people who limit their reading to a single newspaper.
The point I want to make in connection with the economic council that the President of the United States has is that these men do not go around the country exhorting businessmen or labour or anyone else. They play a full time role in economic analysis and they head a fairly large staff of experts who are partly drawn in on a temporary basis, as may be possible under this legislation, to do task force jobs in special fields. In other words, there is an interplay moving in and out. Here is the place where the business economist or the trade unionist economist functions rather, than in the top trio who in a sense are the top experts in their craft.


But one of the points that Mr. Jacoby makes is that it is a mistake if the members of the council represent different schools of economic thought. I can just imagine a council with John Deutsch as chairman and Lome McDougall and Dr. Shrumm from British Columbia as members. You can just see the possibilities of conflict there, and a complete breakdown in this trio really getting things going. I want to suggest to the minister that the three permanent members should have a strong grounding in academic economics, that they should have the reputation of being professional economists and that some effort should be made to see that all three of them have generally the same economic approach. I hope it is not a pre-Keynesian approach such as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) introduced in his budget.
One of the other things I should like to note about the council in the United States is that as a result of the fact that the three of them are generally kept away from what seems to be a favorite activity in Canada, sending people up and down the country to exhort and to stump, they have time to concentrate upon really serious study, and the popularization of what they do comes later when their reports are published and particularly when the president, or in our case the ministry of the government, sets out to popularize and interpret their findings and indicators in a way that can be presented generally and publicly.
There is one feature about the United States set-up that is handy and I think it would be an improvement here. I refer to how long these people should be members of the council. I think they should only be in office at the pleasure of the government, because it seems to me that if, as is quite possible in the Canadian scene, we have a change of government these are three positions in particular that require people in them that will be sympathetic to the objectives of the government. I have grave doubts at the present time whether it is right that the board of broadcast governors should consist of the three personalities who are now there, in view of the fact that I know that on the part of some members of the government at least there is a certain distaste because of their background. I think that particularly in the case of economic analysis you need to have some kind of approach that is not antithetical. Just imagine the Leader of the Opposition being back in power, saddled with a couple of left wing economists and not being able to do anything about it. You can just see the difficulties that would arise. This is a point from the United States experience.

Another point I should like to make with regard to the American experience is that the economists who are picked should have some experience and background in government organization. None of us can judge whether the so-called whiz kid, Stanley, from Toronto and these other fellows, are good economists, but it is quite apparent they do not know very much about government organization or the operations of the Department of National Revenue. In this sense it seems to me that what the government needs to be looking for in the permanent members are economists who have proved by their publications, their addresses, the courses that they teach and their associations that they have some conception of the federal framework of government, at the very least.
One thing that is quite apparent about the economic council of advisers in the United States is that as the years have gone by they have increasingly won the respect of congress itself. I think it is worth while noting this, because congress tends to be very suspicious of any group of advisers which is working primarily for the president. Of course, one of the reasons why congress has been won over to a degree is that the reports are made public and because the council acts as an integrating or co-ordinating authority for all kinds of economic research that is being carried on, including some that is being provided for congressional committees themselves.
One of the cliches that seem to come up in this house is that whenever our friends immediately next to this group mention the idea of money somebody always says, yes, go ahead and print it, and we get the idea of the printing press. Also, whenever we mention planning in our party somebody throws up his hands and says immediately, dictatorship, and we .are heading in a terrible direction.
I should like to say something about the differences and distinctions that the minister drew between indicative and imperative planning. He did not give a complete or thorough review. In this sense it may be that the Leader of the Opposition has a point. The more economic tools we develop, which I suppose will be the chief function of the economic council, the more it becomes apparent that by using these economic tools, by shifting investment and providing incentives here and penalties there, you do move toward control of the economy, and whether it is going to be indicative planning or imperative planning is really a matter of mere semantics rather than any substantial difference.
Economic Council of Canada
I give this example, if hon. members will look at it. The Minister of Finance seems to feel that the most influential item of what still remains in his budget is the incentive to industries to establish in underdeveloped or slow developing economic areas of our country, because of the tax free period. This in essence is a nice, sweet form of incentive; but once you have the kind of economic analysis that leads you to know the whole pattern of possible incentives or penalties with regard to investment, direction of income and employment and the kind of training that people should have it almost becomes a question of playing on this economic machinery like an organ.
I do not think that anyone would say that A. A. Eerie, the American economist, is dangerous or suspect or Marxist, in fact he is famous as an anti-Castro man. In his book ''The American Economic Republic", he makes the point that we have in the United States a managed kind of economy, and that the argument between the so-called laissez faire types and the interventionist types is an unreal one. As we move more and more towards an understanding of the economic system, and such things as input and output tables, and begin to move down to detail about our whole national economy, the more it will become just a question of plugging in or plugging out or pressing here or pressing there. It will require a fairly complex system of penalties and incentives. We have many now, in a disorganized way.
Now, to say that we are moving towards this when we already have it in some fields is a platitude. When there is a big distinction made between so-called indicative planning and imperative planning, it is, it seems to me, nothing more than a piece of sophistry that may be instrumental in keeping the former prime minister off the Liberal government's back. I do not believe it should really deceive anybody.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the New Democratic party, if it could have the economic council of its dreams, would of course take something like this bill and then try to give the council power to frame, more specifically, the kind of measures that would be needed in order to respond to the economic indicators and the long range policies that the economic council recommend. One of the points to which we always need to return when we talk about economists, is to remember that they are not the gods of this world, and that economics is just a means by which each one of us, we hope, and our country, and the world will be made richer. In doing this, the society of today finds its motives and its ambitions, I

Economic Council of Canada think, less and less in the marketplace and in the field of economics, and more and more outside of it.
The minister, in his analysis, made the point with which I agree, that because of the catch-up in post-war demand and the effect of the tremendous productive capacity that followed investments leading up into the midfifties, we have satisfied to quite an extent the main consumer needs in this country. I assume, although he did not say it, that going on from this we need to develop new or additional consumer needs. I suppose the grounds for this are going to develop in what we refer to as the technical and social fields, that is new needs in new equipment, in a better education and a deeper, richer life, if you want to put it that way, through cultural activities, through such things as centennials and an emphasis upon history.
This is really not the field of the economist. It seems to me this is the difficult role of the economic council. If it produces overmuch respect through its operation it may even dominate the climate of thinking in this country about what our goals should be. 'While it is all very well for us to emphasize the economic goals that our society should have, I think all of us today realize that there are many larger ones. This, in a sense, brings in a point made by the former prime minister regarding provincial jurisdictions and provincial problems. I mention this because so many of the provincial responsibilities are not primarily economic. They are educational and they are cultural. In that sense, they are ones which the federal government can never provide.
It seems to me that here is where any interplay needs to take place. It seems to me that the economic management of this country's economy can only be done at the federal level, with any kind of justice. I say this in denial of what some of our friends, including friends of our own party in Quebec seem to feel, that you can establish within the sovereignty of a single state some kind of viable economic system that could go on regardless of the over-all matrix of the economy in the rest of the country. But in the direction of the provincial needs, the economic council, and the members who come to it, it seems to me will be generally charged with the responsibility of translating both what the provinces need and what we need, socially and culturally, for the consideration of the full time people, so that they can better comprehend both what we express in parliament itself and what the needs of our economic system should be.
One of the points made by the leader of the Social Credit party I cannot help mentioning. He seemed to feel that the productivity


council was well on its way to introducing a new period of harmony in management-labour relations. He seems to feel that this is going to be one of the great objectives of the economic council. I want to express right at this time a great scepticism that this is the role or can be the role of the economic council. It seems to me that we have not yet reached the stage, either in the sophistication or organization of Canadian labour union in any national way, when a national economic council could serve as any great instrument for better management-labour relations. It seems to me that is frustrated right off the bat by the division of labour responsibility, federally and provincially.
It is frustrated because of the differing character of so much of the Canadian labour movement, and the fact that the Canadian Labour Congress does not speak for the whole labour movement. I do not believe the congress would want to claim to speak for the whole labour movement. It is quite apparent from the way in which the Canadian Labour Congress has been moving in connection with the difficulties it has with some of its own membership, that we are not at the stage when we can say that, on the national level, we have a coherent labour group with coherent aims and with a single leadership that is prepared to speak for the whole labour movement within the framework of something like the economic council. They could advise, yes. I want to emphasize also that I feel the business community in Canada is really not much better off than the labour community in terms of really being able to express national intentions and wishes of the groups represented on this national economic council. I am not trying to be negative in giving these, in a sense, warnings.
It seems to me this may be important, however, because there may be a tremendous expectation that these 25 people who will be on this economic council, who will be selected to represent farm groups, labour groups and so on, are somehow or other going to give you a real economic forum on the national level that can do things. Well, Mr. Speaker, I do not think they can do them any better than we can do them here in parliament. As advisers, as interlocutors or in a sense liaison people with ideas on the situations out in the country, they can do a fine job. In time, if the economic council develops into the kind of organization and representation that some of these agencies parallel to it have in the United Kingdom, in France or in the United States, then I think it may be time to talk of a new period or a new opportunity in the field of management-labour relations on the national level.

The final remark I would like to make about the economic council is related to what I might say is the left wing or the radical bias that I hope still exists in our party. For years we have claimed, and we believe it, that economic planning is the tool by which Canada can achieve almost anything that it wants in the economic field. Now, when one goes that far you are of course usually asked to spell out in more detail just how this would work out, how it could be done, what would be some of the steps you would take, and what kind of agencies you would create.
Usually there is the spectre, raised by people who do not sympathize with our point of view, that our kind of operation would lead to a great deal of nationalization, and that in a sense we would take over very many industries. I would like to comment here that in his speech on the budget address, and on a number of other occasions, the leader of our party has shown in main outline the kind of steps we would take in the short term to get our economy going again, and in essence the very same principles and ideas would be the ones we would put forward and have advocated by any economic council we would create.
We think the economic council is likely to be a very sterile operation in terms of good or effective advice, if the three people selected for it are the kind of economists who believe in a laissez faire economy, who are afraid to detail a program that an effective government would be prepared to carry out, and which an ineffective government would hesitate in front of, because of the likelihood of causing a storm in one part of the community or another.
The New Democratic party sees this legislation as another very small step along a road that we think is inevitable for this country. We just wish it was a larger stride but we are not complaining about the fact that it is being taken; and later on, if we have the time, other speakers will deal with some of the more specific details.
I was intrigued that the Leader of the Social Credit party and the leader of the official opposition made the point that, as this discussion goes further and as we get into the clauses of the bill, they will, if I may use the metaphor, work like terriers shaking out each clause. We will be very interested in seeing what kind of amendments they present. We believe the bill as it stands is a fairly good one. It does not go as far as we would like, but we are satisfied with it as it is; and aside from possibly one or two small amendments or suggestions we feel the bill should be put into effect as quickly as possible; and we would hope it has very smooth sailing in the next hour or so.

I took from his remarks that, after he went through his analysis of this bill, he really liked it. The only area that he seemed particularly concerned with, and I am not sure this pertains technically to the legislation itself, was the character of the appointees. If these men were not of a calibre that he would like then, according to him, the legislation would not achieve its ends. If, on the other hand, they were, then this legislation is fine.
As I say, this seems to me to be a marked contrast to the type of dissertation we heard with respect to this type of legislation last session. If you have an interruption of substance and intelligence to make, then make it and I will sit down. I will try to answer your questions. Your interruptions are not even appreciated by the members of your own party, the intelligent ones.
I suggest again, sir, that we scrutinize this legislation and that we scrutinize the attitude of hon. members opposite towards it to make sure that this nation, once again, will not be burdened with this notion of planning for the sake of planning. We hope, as most hon. members hope and most Canadians hope that this measure will not mean direction and regimentation which is so alien to the Canadian spirit, the kind of direction and

Economic Council of Canada regimentation that was superimposed on this nation before 1957. We hope it will not mean interference with individual initiative.
The hon. member for Port Arthur might say again that I sound like Barry Gold water. I am not afraid to get up on my feet in this House of Commons and state that the party I support believes that individual initiative, individual dignity still means something in 1963. There are many Canadians from coast to coast who believe that they can make their own way in life, naturally depending to a great extent on government, but not sharing in the collectivist views of the hon. lady from Northumberland or the views expounded by the President of the Privy Council in his book and on the floor of this House of Commons.
I agree fundamentally with most hon. members that no longer can we validly become involved in the old classical debate of free enterprise versus complete state control. We all recognize that this is no longer a valid debate in 1963. I am sorry if I seem to be underlining this fact again and again in my speech, but I believe it does bear repetition. While we should not get involved in this classical debate of free enterprise versus state control I think it is a very valid consideration for hon. members in this chamber, especially when government, whether we like it or not, is getting bigger and bigger, to do some honest, sincere thinking about individual dignity and the rights and freedom of the individual. This is especially true when we are talking about a bill of the basic importance of the one which is before us tonight.
Again, I appeal to the treasury benches opposite, to hon. members opposite, that if this bill is going to have any long or short term effects they must make it readily intelligible to the individual, if it is going to have any meaning at all in pushing our economy forward. In so far as this notion of planning is concerned, let me simply say this, and I think it is perhaps a truism, that we in Canada should be extremely proud of one of the greatest civil services in the western world. It has been my opinion, and I say this in a non-partisan way because I understand that when hon. members opposite did this they did it in a sincere way, that when the Liberal party forms a government they often tend to give the civil service jobs to do that they should not have to do, and which they often do not want to do. I said in another debate that Haldane said justice must not only be just, but it must be seen to be just. This is, in essence what he said. I refer to this because an administration which is made up of nine ex-senior bureaucrats must spell out

in detail what it means by planning if it is not going to be held suspect by the Canadian people from coast to coast.
Now, sir, the last principle that is involved in this bill and which I should like to discuss on second reading relates to the notion of consultation, which is a central principle in the bill. I am glad that hon. members opposite realize the necessity for consultation. I thought they were going to get off to a good start when I listened to the throne speech. They talked about co-operative federalism. All of us on this side of the house know that co-operative federalism denotes a high degree of consultation with the provinces.
Well, what has happened so far, Mr. Speaker?
One of the basic reasons that the whole economic policy of this government is floundering on the rocks is the lack of consultation. The Minister of Finance did not consult his officials; he consulted three experts outside his department. We have seen what happened to the budget as a result of lack of consultation. The Minister of Finance, and the members on the treasury benches, forgot to consult the provinces regarding the central aspect of their short term economic program. The Minister of Finance went on television, then he came to the floor of this house, and he said the municipal loan fund legislation was the key short term measure of their economic program to stimulate the economy. It would make jobs available immediately, he said. Before we announced the municipal winter works program, we consulted the provinces. What has happened? The whole short term program of the government is floundering because of lack of consultation. The budget floundered because of lack of consultation. I put questions to the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) whether he consulted with the Minister of Finance regarding exemptions on building materials when he said there would be a $500 bonus given to people building houses in the winter months. We find that even members of the cabinet are not consulting each other, but I am glad that finally in this bill they realize the importance of the principle of consultation. Consultation often involves nothing more than courtesy.
I am not going to inform the house tonight whether I am taking the centralizing point of view or whether I am arguing for provincial rights. That is absolutely immaterial. But I can say that in 1963, things being what they are in this federal union of ours called Canada, no matter how much centralization the Minister of Finance advocates, I hope before he convinces the cabinet that certain legislation is good for the short term, someone, possibly a minister from Quebec or possibly

a minister from British Columbia, or any other province will tell him that consulting with the provinces, even by telephone occasionally, is a very handy thing to do.
The throne speech spoke of co-operative federalism and consultation. By their fruits ye shall know them; and I hope that the notion of consultation in this bill will really mean something. Just the other day the Prime Minister told the Canadian people his government wanted to get on immediately with the municipal loan fund legislation; but the President of the Privy Council, outside of this house, announced that we were in no hurry, that Mr. Lesage is correct and that we are going to wait. It seems to me that the centralizers do not consult those who believe in co-operative federalism in this new cabinet.
One of the real problems, and I regard it in a very optimistic nature, facing Canada today involves federal-provincial relations. Every Canadian of good will, no matter what party he belongs to, hopes that before 1967 many of the basic problems involving federal-provincial relations will be solved so that our centenary will be a true celebration for all Canadians from coast to coast.

subtopic: APPROVAL OP CERTAIN AUTHORIZED EXPENDITURES FOR FISCAL YEAR 1962-1963
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps I could say a word or two in connection with the suggestion of the house leader. I certainly concur with what he suggested. I assume that the bill will be available to us tomorrow, and not in the mail box on Saturday, after we have passed the resolution. Hon. members realize

full well that this resolution embodies a discussion of financial expenditures made over the past year and it would be open to the committee dealing with the resolution to deal with it in an hour, or a day, or a month and ask a great many questions in connection with it.
The only qualification I would make to the agreement which has been made is that after second reading it does not necessarily follow-it may, but it does not necessarily follow-that we will go into committee and deal with the committee stage forthwith, because we may need to ask more questions and we may require some time in order to ascertain the detail which we would have ascertained at the resolution stage and which we will now deal with in committee of the whole following second reading.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: APPROVAL OP CERTAIN AUTHORIZED EXPENDITURES FOR FISCAL YEAR 1962-1963
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) has just informed me that he will have ready for tabling in the morning-I have a proof copy now-the report on supply, which contains everything of substance that will appear in the bill. It is not in the form of a bill. I cannot say just how fast, following first reading, the bills will be produced, but they will be produced just as fast as it is possible for the printing bureau to print them. I will take every possible step to see they are distributed as quickly as possible. I think that really all the essential detail will be found in the report on supply, which I understand will be available for distribution immediately it is tabled at 11 o'clock tomorrow.

subtopic: APPROVAL OP CERTAIN AUTHORIZED EXPENDITURES FOR FISCAL YEAR 1962-1963
speechtext: I quite appreciate the statement of the house leader. I think that report will probably contain most of the details, if not all of them. As long as we have an understanding that we do not have to go through committee of the whole immediately following second reading.

whether the house leader would give us a forecast of the business that will be before us tomorrow and such days as he can indicate for next week.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I will be very happy to do that, sir. Tomorrow, once we have disposed of the committee stage, concerning

Business of the House
which I understand there is a general disposition to regard as a formality preceding the appropriation bill, and had the first reading of the bill, we will take the estimates of the Department of Transport and, I pray, dispose of them during the day. On Monday it is proposed to take, as the first item of business, the appropriation bill which will be given first reading tomorrow and to proceed with it until it has been disposed of, and then to resume the debate on the economic council.
We would, of course, be very happy if both these measures could be disposed of on Monday. But in any event I think it would be the intention of the government to begin on Tuesday the budget resolutions, starting with the resolution respecting the customs tariff. What will be done on subsequent days of the week, I am not able to forecast sufficiently accurately at the moment to make it worth while communicating to the house.
